Engineering

Built and maintained the systems and pages the product runs on: the equipment data model, six production web pages, and a set of specialist AI agents.

 0
Models fully documented, with source materials found and verified across 6 equipment categories

What it was

A small team of interns built a master reference library of building equipment manufacturers and model families, including chillers, air handlers, boilers, and generators. Every entry follows the same data schema — manufacturer, model, manual, warranty terms, parts catalog, and preventive maintenance template — so records stay consistent and queryable across categories. This became the data behind the platform's equipment records.

Four documents, every single model

Documenting one model family was never a single lookup. Each of the 260 models I owned called for its own manufacturer manual, its own warranty terms, its own parts catalog, and its own preventive maintenance template, each one tracked down and checked on its own. Where one could not be found, the goal was a reasonable substitute rather than an empty field, so the real research effort works out to roughly 1,040 documents across six equipment categories, not 260.

My contribution

  • I owned research and documentation for six equipment categories: fan coil units, VAV boxes, generators, UPS systems, switchgear, and transformers.
  • I sourced and verified the manual, warranty, parts, and maintenance template links for each model family across five manufacturers per category.
  • When a model listing was unclear, I flagged it for follow up instead of guessing.

Tools

Built using ChatGPT, Google Sheets, manufacturer documentation, and manual research.

Webpages fully developed and filled out: Protect, Perform, Activate IQ, Apt and Condo, Student, and Senior
The Protect page as it looks live today. This is one of the pages I spent the most time on.

What it was

This project ran on two tracks at once, not sequentially: a page by page mobile responsiveness check across the marketing site, and a detailed desktop revision pass fixing punctuation, layout, imagery, and messaging clarity on the product pages. Checking both viewports in parallel meant fixes were verified on mobile before they shipped, not retrofitted afterward. I spent most of my time on Protect, Perform, and Activate IQ, then carried the same fixes through the Apartments and Condos, Student Housing, and Senior Living pages.

Protect and Perform, before and after

On the old site, Protect and Perform were each a single word in one shared homepage list, with no page of their own. Today, Protect has its own page built around three ideas: work orders that route themselves to the right vendor, a structure built for property buildings instead of generic field service, and pattern detection that flags a recurring equipment fault before it becomes a bigger problem. Perform has its own page built around location verified completions, one shared operational record for field teams and vendors, and intelligence that feeds back into the platform.

Two specific rewrites were mine: I replaced a placeholder AI routed example with a more accurate one, and I rewrote the legacy system comparison so it reflects a real system that is a few years old, not an exaggerated stereotype from decades back.

My contribution

  • I completed the mobile check on 13 core pages, covering product pages, industry pages, and company pages, and verified layout on mobile viewports.
  • I fully developed and filled out six major webpages: Protect, Perform, Activate IQ, Apt and Condo, Student, and Senior. The tracking sheet captured 48 assigned wording, content, layout, branding, and image updates; I completed 45 of them.
  • I also developed and improved additional sections that were not listed on the tracking sheet, including visual systems, imagery, layout, and explanatory content across the six pages.
  • In an internal review, my page level work was recognized as the strongest on the site.

Additional sections developed beyond the punch list

Much of the page development was not captured on the tracking sheet. I restyled the legacy system mockups on three pages so they read as a real system from a few years back instead of an exaggerated stereotype, swapped a generic stock photo for a more specific engineering image, recolored a plain black and white QR code, and rebuilt a cramped, overlapping section into full width panels that actually explain the idea. Between the tracked items and this additional work, roughly 20 style, graphic, and section-level improvements shipped across the six pages.

Tools

Used Claude, ChatGPT, browser developer tools, Google Sheets, and the CMS.

Specialist agents I owned end to end, out of 26 in Activate's agentic framework

Why the agents matter

Activate's broader agent framework covers 26 specialist agents across the platform; I owned 9 of them end to end. Each agent gives Activate focused domain judgment for a specific operational problem. The expertise layer teaches the model how to classify issues, apply standards, make decisions, report clearly, and escalate risk before live-data integrations are added.

What they cover

  • Service Request: classify, route, and escalate tenant or building requests.
  • Preventive Maintenance: identify missed work, schedule risk, and recurring issues.
  • Equipment Lifecycle: assess asset condition and repair-versus-replacement timing.
  • COI and Supplier: flag insurance, vendor, performance, and compliance risk.
  • Deficiency and Compliance: prioritize unresolved conditions and requirements.
  • Visitor and Access Control: support secure check-in, access decisions, and exception handling.

Three files per agent

Each of the nine agents received a cited domain-research document, a detailed skill document covering knowledge, decision logic, output format, and a worked example, plus a prompt defining identity, accuracy, reporting style, and escalation. That produced 27 files in total.

Tools

Claude Projects, current web research, named industry standards, and realistic Activate report data for testing.

03

Business & Strategy

Researched the market Activate sells into: how competitors' platforms work today, and who the target buyers are across 20 U.S. metros.

 0
Detailed screenshots captured across PRISM by Building Engines

What it was

This was a hands on competitive audit of PRISM, a property management platform built by Building Engines. I walked through the live product and captured how it handles the same functional areas our platform covers, then wrote up the findings as a 25-page internal report: page-by-page comparisons, a master scorecard across 40+ website and product dimensions, and a prioritized list of fixes, ranked by expected impact on buyer trust and conversion.

My contribution

  • I captured 196 screenshots across the competitor platform, documenting page-level and multi-step workflow detail in areas such as accounting, equipment, properties, users, inspections, preventive maintenance, work orders, communications, and reporting.
  • I organized the screenshots into a shared reference library so the product team could compare it against our own workflows.
  • I wrote the findings up as a structured report: what each site does well, where Activate has real gaps (case studies, pricing signals, product screenshots, AI governance detail), and where Activate's writing and positioning already beat the competitor's.
  • I cropped screenshots for efficient review while ensuring important features, controls, and workflow details remained recorded and visible.

Tools

Used screenshot capture, Google Drive, and feature comparison notes.

Evidence

The 25-page written analysis I produced from the screenshots: page-by-page findings, a master scorecard across 40+ dimensions, and a prioritized fix list.
